clue.text: Entertainers that won't perform unless they're given a hand

definitions.text: Entertainers that won't perform unless they're given a hand

blocks.clueFragment: Entertainers that won't perform unless they're given a hand
blocks.note: surface reading: prima donna performers who refuse to go on without applause
setter's reading: these performers only come alive when a human hand is literally pushed inside them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Given a hand' normally means applauded; here it means a puppeteer's hand slides inside the figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand-operated fabric figures are a classic children's show act, so they count as performers who need a hand.

clue.text: Using fewer fossil fuels, meagre energy's provided?

indicators.note: the phrase that follows provides, or supplies, the letters straight from its own spelling

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and most of the second

explanation.surface: Someone notes that cutting back on coal and oil leaves a household with only a meagre energy supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside meaGRE ENERgy; 'meagre' tempts you to look for a word like LEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Green is the everyday term for environmentally friendly, and the comparative describes lower reliance on coal, oil and gas.

clue.text: Little surgical procedure – time for work in theatre

blocks.note: op is the short, 'little' form of operation
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A minor operation, and then it's time to get to work in the operating theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre looks like the surgical one, but the definition points to the opera house stage.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a dramatic musical composition staged in a theatre, so it is a stage work.

clue.text: 25 times reserved, but not in or on display

indicators.note: 'but not' excludes something, so a piece of the word just given is taken away

blocks.note: the answer to 25 is ECHO, the radio alphabet's code word for E
x is the multiplication sign
a reserved person is shy and held back
taken as written, and removed from the front of the previous word

explanation.surface: Twenty-five times something was booked, yet it never went in or on show.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is to 25 down, ECHO, which in the NATO alphabet is E. INHIBITED loses IN to leave HIBITED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exhibited has been shown publicly, as in a gallery, so the past participle matches being displayed.

clue.text: Free gun dog, absolutely no good

indicators.note: 'absolutely no' means none at all, so every instance of a letter is stripped out

blocks.note: a gundog is a dog trained to retrieve game for shooters; that the result also sits inside these words is a coincidence of the deletion
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A gun dog that has been let loose proves completely useless.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Gs in GUNDOG go, which is why the clue says 'absolutely'.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a knot or a fastening is to loosen it, releasing whatever was tied, so the verbs match.

clue.text: Possible destination for 15 men on board, on short journey

blocks.note: pawns are chessmen, the pieces on the board
a hop is a brief trip

explanation.surface: Fifteen crew members aboard a ship head off on a brief trip somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 across is BORROWER, someone who might go to a pawnbroker for cash; '15 men' suggests a rugby team but the number belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone short of money takes valuables to a pawnbroker's premises for a loan, so it is where a cadger might go.

clue.text: Rolling broadcast in list after cutting is experimental

indicators.note: cutting removes part of something, so letters are lopped out of the word
one item goes inside another, so letters sit within the shortened word
something rolling turns over, so the whole result is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut from the previous word
to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: A rolling news broadcast squeezed into the schedule after edits is something new being tested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' looks like a link word joining definition to wordplay, but it is the piece cut away. The reversal applies to the whole construction, not just the broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial run or trial version is a test of something new, and the noun works attributively like an adjective.

clue.text: Last recourse of washer-upper, seeing terrible lot we ate?

indicators.note: something terrible is a mess, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The person doing the dishes despairs at the enormous pile left by everything the family ate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last recourse' is a playful way of saying the final thing used, after washing and rinsing.
explanation.definitionFit: After washing comes drying, so the cloth for drying dishes is literally the final item a dishwasher reaches for.

clue.text: End of plodding Queen cover's cut – it should soar

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
a thing cut in is inserted between two parts, splitting what surrounds it

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword abbreviation for the Queen
a lid covers a pot or box

explanation.surface: At the end of a slow innings the Queen's cover drive is cut short, yet the ball ought to fly high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' and 'cut' suggest cricket shots, but here the cover goes in between the first two pieces. ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: An engineless aircraft rides rising air currents, so soaring is exactly what such a craft is built for.

clue.text: It's taken from its pot and put on the lid

definitions.text: It's taken from its pot and put on the lid

blocks.clueFragment: It's taken from its pot and put on the lid
blocks.note: surface reading: something in a kitchen pot whose lid gets put back on top
setter's reading: the lid is an eyelid, and the pot is a little cosmetics pot

explanation.walkthrough: The pot and lid conjure cooking; they are a make-up compact and an eyelid.
explanation.definitionFit: Coloured powder for the eyelids is scooped from a small cosmetic container and brushed on, matching the clue exactly.

clue.text: Dream of London's East End I would restore

indicators.note: Cockney speech of the East End drops the initial aitch, so that letter is lost

blocks.note: I'd is the contraction of 'I would'
to heal is to restore to health

explanation.surface: Someone's dream is to bring London's East End back to its former glory.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney, the accent of London's East End, HEAL is said 'EAL. The East End is the traditional working-class area of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream holiday or dream home is the perfect one, so as a modifier it matches the adjective meaning perfect.

clue.text: Yobs roared "No retreating", scrapped occasionally at close quarters

indicators.note: letters scrapped at intervals means every other one goes, leaving the rest
retreating means going backwards, so the kept letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Hooligans shouted that nobody would back down, and they brawled now and then at close range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No retreating' looks like a chant, but 'No' is fodder and 'retreating' applies to the selected letters of all three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at close quarters is very close by, so the adverb for a short distance away fits.

clue.text: 13's equivalent to 10's spread ...

indicators.note: things spread out are scattered about, so these letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
10 across is IDEAL, and the apostrophe s adds an S

explanation.surface: A cross-referencing clue saying one entry matches another's spread, leading on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 across is REMOTE, so the definition asks for a synonym of it; '10's' supplies IDEAL plus S.
explanation.definitionFit: A remote village and an isolated village are the same thing: far from others, cut off.

clue.text: ... opposite to 11 – one could facilitate viewing

definitions.note: a noun phrase for the device, while the first sense is an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: 11 across is NEARBY, and its opposite is far away
second meaning: the handset used to change television channels

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 12, but this clue stands alone; 11 across is NEARBY.
explanation.definitionFit: Far-off places are distant from here, and a television controller lets you switch channels from your sofa.

clue.text: Called out phoney, an evil snake

indicators.note: something called out is spoken, so what counts is the sound of the words

blocks.note: mock means phoney, a sin is an evil

explanation.surface: Someone is publicly denounced as a fake and a wicked serpent in human form.
explanation.walkthrough: MOCK + A + SIN said together gives the snake's name; 'snake' looks like an insult for a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The water moccasin, or cottonmouth, is a venomous pit viper of the southern United States.

clue.text: One cadges what's saved by Andrew or Robert in recession?

indicators.note: what is saved is held safely within, so the letters are kept inside the words
a recession is a going back, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of the first name, the middle word and the start of the second name

explanation.surface: Wondering which of two men, Andrew or Robert, has savings to lend during an economic downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: andREW OR ROBert, read backwards. 'Recession' looks economic but is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To cadge is to scrounge or take on loan, so a person who cadges is someone taking things on loan.

clue.text: Repeatedly criticise Sunday lunch?

blocks.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly
the clue asks for criticise a second time, and to beef is to complain

explanation.surface: Someone keeps grumbling about the traditional weekend family meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repeatedly' asks for two words for criticise in a row. The Sunday roast is the traditional British weekend lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint of roasted cattle meat is the classic British Sunday lunch, so the dish stands for the meal.

clue.text: Currently on the up, Yankee in blue advanced and came first

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another sits within its letters
in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the whole is reversed

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the radio alphabet
feeling blue is feeling sad
A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A level
to come first in a race is to win it

explanation.surface: An American sportsman in a blue kit is on the rise, having gone forward and won.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currently on the up' looks like one phrase meaning trending, but it splits after the definition, and 'on the up' reverses everything that follows in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words refer to the present time, as opposed to the past, so the adverbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Set to get new or old pence, apparently

definitions.text: to get new or old pence, apparently
definitions.note: a whimsical verb-phrase reading of the noun

blocks.note: first meaning: the painted scenery at the rear of a stage

blocks.clueFragment: to get new or old pence, apparently
blocks.note: second meaning, read cryptically: choose D, the old penny, and discard P, the new penny

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as BACK D, DROP P: in old British money d stood for a penny; decimal pence are p.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre set includes the painted cloth hung behind the actors, and the playful reading backs one penny symbol over another.

clue.text: British ought to undermine European act

indicators.note: in a down entry, undermining means going underneath, so this piece is placed below

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
E is the abbreviation for European
'have to' means ought to, must

explanation.surface: A Eurosceptic claim that Britain should sabotage a European law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' looks like a noun, a piece of legislation, but it is the verb for conducting oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: To behave is to conduct yourself in a certain manner, the same sense as acting well or badly.

clue.text: Summons to fight everyone in competition

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside its letters

blocks.note: all means everyone
a cup is a knockout competition

explanation.surface: All the players in a tournament are challenged to a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to fight' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A call-up is an order to join the armed forces, a summons to military service.

clue.text: What gets any temp working?

indicators.note: working implies operating on something, so the letters are reworked into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking what motivates a temporary worker to get on with the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a temp works for wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Temporary staff are hired by the hour, so wages are what motivates them to turn up and work.

clue.text: Hard area to land in agreed with spin bowler – maybe ...

definitions.note: an example of the category, flagged by 'maybe'

indicators.note: spinning things whirl round, so the letters are tumbled into a new order

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
A is the abbreviation for area
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cricket talk: a tough patch of pitch where the ball should land, agreed with the spin bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes 'bowler' look like a player; it is the hat, an example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowler is a hard round felt hat, one example of things worn on the head.

clue.text: Husband sounded in a state

indicators.note: sounded means spoken aloud, so the word is identified by how it is pronounced

blocks.note: to husband resources is to conserve them, and to garner is to gather and store

explanation.surface: A married man made a noise while in a heightened emotional state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Husband' is a verb here, not a man, and in a non-rhotic British accent GARNER and the country sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The West African republic is a sovereign nation, and a country is a state in the political sense.

clue.text: ... kind of wicket requiring "twitch" described by broadcaster

indicators.note: to describe a shape around something is to draw round it, so one piece encircles the other

blocks.note: a tic is an involuntary twitch
Sky is a British satellite broadcaster

explanation.surface: A cricket pitch on which batting brings on a nervous twitch, as the TV commentator puts it.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is the UK satellite TV company that covers cricket. A sticky wicket is a damp pitch drying awkwardly in the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: A sticky wicket is a cricket pitch that is difficult to bat on, hence a tricky situation in idiom.

clue.text: Creature climbing up under arch

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading from the bottom upwards
in a down entry, being under means being placed below the other piece

blocks.note: arch means playfully sly or coy
taken as written

explanation.surface: An animal scrambling up beneath a stone arch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch' looks like a structure but is the adjective for knowingly playful.
explanation.definitionFit: The coypu is a large South American aquatic rodent, so it is an example of a creature.

clue.text: Mirror becoming regional paper?

blocks.note: first meaning: to imitate or reflect, as a verb
second meaning: a title used by several local newspapers, such as the Liverpool one

explanation.surface: A national tabloid, the Daily Mirror, turning into a local newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic Mirror suggests the national tabloid; it is really the verb. The Liverpool Echo and Northern Echo are British regional papers.
explanation.definitionFit: To reflect or repeat something is to copy it back, and several provincial British newspapers carry this title.

clue.text: There it is, five-nil, Italy against the French

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
O looks like a zero
I is the international vehicle code for Italy
la is a French word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A football commentator triumphantly announcing a five-nil scoreline for Italy over France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Five-nil' and 'against' paint a match, but each word is just a letter source.
explanation.definitionFit: The borrowed French exclamation announces a reveal, used like 'here you are' when presenting something.

clue.text: Standard cheap tyre burst

indicators.note: something burst is broken apart, so these letters fly into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A budget tyre suffered the usual blowout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' reads as an adjective in the surface, but the definition is the noun meaning a model to copy.
explanation.definitionFit: An archetype is the original pattern or model, and a standard is likewise a benchmark against which others are measured.

clue.text: Mix of raisins put into tropical treat

indicators.note: a mix is a jumble, so these letters are stirred together into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A handful of mixed raisins is stirred into an exotic dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' belongs to the fodder, not to the indicator phrase 'Mix of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The wrinkled purple fruit grows in tropical climates and is eaten as a sweet, fragrant delicacy.
